codes.label: Care recipient's own wishes and dignity
codes.definition: The parent's own preferences, autonomy, privacy, and sense of dignity (including whether they would rather be cared for by a child or by outsiders, and how much say they can still meaningfully have) should be asked about directly and weighed, ideally while they can still express them.

codes.label: Medical needs and safety risks
codes.definition: The actual level of hands-on, skilled, or supervisory care required (falls, medications, transfers, wandering, nighttime supervision) and whether each option can safely provide it.

codes.label: Prognosis and how needs will change
codes.definition: Recovery after a stroke or progression of dementia is uncertain and uneven, so the choice should be judged against likely future needs and a worse-case trajectory, not just the current snapshot or the minimum estimate.

codes.label: Caregiver capacity and burnout
codes.definition: The caregiver's own physical, emotional, and social capacity to sustain daily care without exhaustion, resentment, isolation, or harm to their health and the care they can give.

codes.label: Caregiver's work, career and professional standing
codes.definition: Whether the caregiver's job, income, benefits, licensure, skills, or career momentum can survive the arrangement, including leave protections, remote or flexible work, and the cost of an extended absence.

codes.label: Cost comparison and finances of each option
codes.definition: The full financial picture of each path: wages and benefits lost, retirement contributions, rent or housing costs, fees and extra charges, home modifications, and the true total rather than headline figures.

codes.label: Funding runway and what happens when money runs out
codes.definition: The care recipient's savings last only a finite period (about a year or four years), so the person should plan for the funding cliff, longer-than-expected need, and who ends up as the backstop.

codes.label: Public benefits, insurance and tax or asset implications
codes.definition: Eligibility for Medicare, Medicaid, veterans benefits, long-term care insurance, local aging programs, and tax or asset-treatment effects that could reduce costs or constrain options, often needing professional advice.

codes.label: Legal and medical documentation and planning
codes.definition: Powers of attorney, healthcare proxies, advance directives, wills, and professional medical or care-manager assessments should be in place or obtained, especially while the parent still has capacity.

codes.label: Reversibility and trial periods
codes.definition: Some options are far harder to undo than others (quitting a job and moving, or moving a parent into one's home), so favoring reversible, phased, or trial arrangements with set review points preserves flexibility.

codes.label: Hybrid and middle-path options
codes.definition: The choice need not be all-or-nothing: part-time aides, adult day programs, respite care, shortened or partial leave, remote work, or combining paid help with visits can meet needs while limiting costs.

codes.label: Long-term planning and exit conditions
codes.definition: The person should look beyond the first months, deciding in advance what would trigger a change in plan, avoiding a temporary arrangement drifting into permanence, and anticipating the next stage of care.

codes.label: Impact on household, marriage and own relationships
codes.definition: The arrangement affects the caregiver's spouse, household routines, privacy, romantic prospects, friendships, and social life, and a spouse's availability or willingness matters a great deal.

codes.label: Parent-child relationship and family dynamics
codes.definition: Shifting from child to caregiver can change the bond with the parent, and returning to the family home may reopen old dynamics or identity questions, so the person should consider how to preserve the relationship.

codes.label: Support from siblings, relatives and community
codes.definition: Other family, friends, neighbors, and community services could share the load, and an offer of support from a distant sibling should be converted into concrete, specific help rather than counted as practical relief.

codes.label: Only-child or sole-caregiver burden
codes.definition: With no one to rotate with or share decisions and guilt, the sole caregiver bears the whole responsibility and needs a backup plan if they become ill or depleted.

codes.label: Quality and reliability of paid care or facility
codes.definition: Whether hired aides or a facility are staffed, trained, licensed, dementia-capable, consistent, and able to handle turnover, backup coverage, and growing needs, including the oversight burden of managing them.

codes.label: Home suitability and safety modifications
codes.definition: Whether the home in question can be made safe and accessible (stairs, bathrooms, grab bars, sightlines, monitoring), at what cost and effort, and whether the current home could be made safe as a stopgap.

codes.label: Proximity, logistics and visiting
codes.definition: Distance affects emergency response, monitoring, visits, appointments, and transportation, and the practical costs of moving, managing a current home or lease, or maintaining two households.

codes.label: Caregiver's clinical expertise as asset and risk
codes.definition: A caregiver's professional training can help judge recovery and care quality, but may also tempt overinvolvement, constant second-guessing, or clinical supervision that strains the relationship.

codes.label: Quality of life, familiarity and social needs
codes.definition: Familiar surroundings versus new environments, disorientation from relocation, social contact, activities, and independence all shape how well the care recipient does in each setting.

codes.label: Long-term regret and personal values
codes.definition: The person should weigh which choice they could live with years later, reflecting their own life goals and values rather than guilt or obligation, including what the decision costs them personally.
